title: Senior's toolkit: transactions, locks and blocking
summary: Isolation levels per transaction, row locks for queues, finding who blocks whom, and timeouts that stop a stuck transaction from taking the site down.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: transactions, locks and blocking
steps.body: When checkouts hang or deadlocks fill the log, these are what an experienced engineer reaches for, in PostgreSQL first, then SQL Server and SQLite.

toolkit.what: PostgreSQL: raise the isolation level for one transaction only, where it is needed, instead of for the whole database. Be ready to retry on `40001`.
flags: the default: each statement sees what was committed before it started
one snapshot for the whole transaction; lost updates fail with 40001
as if transactions ran one at a time; catches write skew; retry on 40001

toolkit.what: Lock the rows you read until commit; skip rows another worker has locked. The standard way to build a job queue on a table (PostgreSQL 9.5+, MySQL 8.0+).
flags: fail at once instead of waiting
leave locked rows out of the result
a weaker lock that does not block inserts referencing the row

toolkit.cmd: SELECT pid, pg_blocking_pids(pid), wait_event_type, state, query FROM pg_stat_activity
toolkit.what: PostgreSQL: who is waiting, and on which process. `idle in transaction` with an old `xact_start` is the classic culprit: an app that opened a transaction and never finished it.
flags: the pids holding the locks this one waits for
a transaction left open, holding its locks
how long the transaction has been open
cancel its query / end its session

toolkit.what: PostgreSQL: give up waiting for a lock after 3 seconds instead of queueing forever. Pair it with `statement_timeout` for slow queries and `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` for abandoned transactions.
flags: max run time of one statement (error 57014)
end sessions that sit in an open transaction
toolkit.example:
ALTER ROLE checkout_app SET lock_timeout = '3s';
ALTER ROLE checkout_app SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '30s';

toolkit.what: PostgreSQL setting: log every lock wait longer than `deadlock_timeout` (1s by default), with who held the lock. Turns "the site was slow at 19:02" into evidence.
flags: how long to wait before checking for a deadlock; also the log threshold
toolkit.example:
ALTER SYSTEM SET log_lock_waits = on;
SELECT pg_reload_conf();

toolkit.cmd: SELECT session_id, blocking_session_id, wait_type, wait_time FROM sys.dm_exec_requests
toolkit.what: SQL Server: the live view of blocking. Follow `blocking_session_id` to the head of the chain. Deadlock graphs are kept in the built-in `system_health` Extended Events session.
flags: requests that are waiting on another session

toolkit.cmd: ALTER DATABASE Tickets SET READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON;
toolkit.what: SQL Server: make READ COMMITTED read row versions instead of waiting for writers, so reports stop blocking checkouts (and the other way round). Already on in Azure SQL Database. It needs a moment with no other connections.
flags: readers see the last committed version, no shared locks
enables the separate SNAPSHOT level (update conflicts raise error 3960)
toolkit.example: ALTER DATABASE Tickets SET READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON WITH ROLLBACK IMMEDIATE;

toolkit.what: SQLite: wait up to 5 seconds for the write lock instead of failing at once with `database is locked`. With `journal_mode = WAL`, readers and the single writer no longer block each other.
flags: milliseconds to retry when the database is locked
write-ahead log: readers keep reading during a write
take the write lock at the start of the transaction

steps.prompt: Checkouts for one event hang for minutes, then time out. `pg_stat_activity` shows this. What do you do first?
code: 31877 | {}         | idle in transaction | 00:14:02   | SELECT seats_left FROM events WHERE id = 5 FOR UPDATE
32010 | {31877}    | active              | 00:02:41   | SELECT seats_left FROM events WHERE id = 5 FOR UPDATE
32044 | {31877}    | active              | 00:02:38   | SELECT seats_left FROM events WHERE id = 5 FOR UPDATE
options: End session 31877 with `pg_terminate_backend(31877)`, then find the code path that opens a transaction and never commits, and set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`
Kill sessions 32010 and 32044, they are the ones running
steps.explain: Session 31877 locked the row 14 minutes ago and has been idle ever since: everyone else queues behind it. Ending it releases the lock now; the timeout and the bug fix (usually an exception path that skips commit or dispose) stop it happening again.

steps.prompt: Stop the checkout role from ever waiting more than 3 seconds for a lock in PostgreSQL.
steps.explain: `lock_timeout` limits waiting for locks. `deadlock_timeout` only says when to check for deadlocks, `statement_timeout` limits total run time, and `busy_timeout` is SQLite.

steps.prompt: Match each error to its meaning.
pairs: deadlock detected: this transaction was rolled back
another connection holds the write lock (SQLITE_BUSY)

steps.prompt: Users report checkouts hanging. Put the investigation in order.
lines: Find waiting sessions and what blocks them (pg_stat_activity with pg_blocking_pids)
Look at the head blocker: its state, how long its transaction has been open, its last query
Release the blockage (cancel or terminate the head blocker)
Find and fix the code path that held the lock too long
Add timeouts (lock_timeout, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout) and log_lock_waits so it fails fast and leaves evidence

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Push the check into the write (`UPDATE ... WHERE seats_left >= 1`), keep transactions short and lock rows in a fixed order, retry only 40001, 40P01 and 1205, and put timeouts on every application role so one stuck transaction fails fast instead of taking the site down.
